blocks.prompt: The Lobster That Climbs Out of Itself
blocks.text: A lobster wears its bones on the outside. Its hard shell is like a suit of armor. But armor cannot grow. So the lobster does something strange. It cracks its shell open at the back. Then it backs out of it, slowly, like pulling off a wet sock. Underneath is a new soft shell. The lobster hides in the rocks until the new shell gets hard. Then it eats the old shell. That is not rude. The old shell is full of what the new one needs.

blocks.prompt: The Lobster That Tastes With Its Feet
blocks.text: A lobster does not have a nose, and it does not have a tongue. It still finds its dinner in the dark. Tiny hairs cover a lobster's legs and feet. Those hairs taste. When a lobster walks across the sea floor, it is tasting every step. Short feelers on its head work like a nose. The lobster flicks them through the water, quick and light, the way you sniff. Look at its two claws. They do not match. One is thick and blunt, with bumps for crushing shells. The other is thin and sharp, for tearing soft food into strips. Some lobsters have the crusher on the right. Some have it on the left. It depends on which claw they used most when they were small. The strangest part comes next. A lobster has no teeth in its mouth. Its teeth are inside its stomach. Three hard plates sit there and grind the food after the lobster swallows it. Scientists call this the gastric mill. One more thing. Lobster blood is not red. It is a pale blue.

blocks.prompt: The Animal That Has to Leave Its Body Behind
blocks.text: Growth is easy for you. Your bones lengthen a little at a time, and your skin stretches to keep up. A lobster cannot do that. Its skeleton is on the outside, a jointed case of shell that protects everything soft, and shell does not stretch. To get bigger, a lobster has to leave its whole body behind. The process is called molting, and it is dangerous. First the lobster takes on water and swells until the shell splits across the back, where the tail meets the body. Then it reverses out through the crack. The hardest part is the claws. A claw is wide and the joint it must pass through is narrow, so in the days beforehand the lobster shrinks the muscle inside the claw, thinning it down until the whole thing can be drawn out like a hand from a glove. What crawls free is a lobster with no armor at all. For a week or more its new shell is soft as wet paper, and every hungry thing on the sea floor knows it. So the lobster wedges itself under a rock and waits. When it is safe, it eats its old shell to reclaim the minerals inside. Molting has a bonus. A lobster that lost a claw to a fight or a fisherman can regrow it, small at first, larger with each molt, until it matches the other one again. Young lobsters molt many times a year. Old ones may go years between molts, growing slowly, getting heavy. The largest one ever recorded weighed about forty-four pounds and came up off the coast of Nova Scotia in 1977.

blocks.prompt: The Food Nobody Wanted
blocks.text: Walk into a restaurant today and the lobster is the most expensive line on the menu. Three hundred years ago, on the same coastline, it was the food you served to people who could not refuse it. When European colonists arrived in New England, lobsters were everywhere. Early accounts describe storms piling them onto the beaches in drifts two feet deep. People gathered them by hand at low tide, no boat required. Something that common could not be valuable. Colonists fed lobster to prisoners, to servants, and to the poor. They ground it up and spread it on fields as fertilizer. There are stories of indentured servants in Massachusetts pushing back, and of contracts limiting how often a household could serve lobster to the people working in it. Lobster was not a treat. It was what you ate when there was nothing else. Two inventions changed its reputation. The first was the can. In the 1840s, canneries along the Maine coast began packing lobster meat in tin, and inland Americans who had never seen the ocean tasted it for the first time. The second was the train. Railroad dining cars served lobster to passengers crossing the country, and those passengers had no idea it was considered garbage back east. They only knew it was delicious and that they had eaten it somewhere fancy. Demand climbed. Prices climbed with it. By the 1880s, lobster was a luxury, and the people who had once been forced to eat it could no longer afford it. The lesson is not really about lobster. It is about how we decide what something is worth. Nothing about the animal changed. Its shell, its claws, its sweet white tail meat were exactly the same in 1700 as in 1900. What changed was who was eating it and what story they told about it. Scarcity and distance did the rest. Today Maine's lobster fishery is careful with what it once wasted. Fishermen measure every catch. Too small goes back. Too large goes back too, because the biggest lobsters lay the most eggs. A female carrying eggs gets a notch cut into her tail, a mark that means release me, and it follows her for years.

blocks.prompt: The Lobster That Does Not Know How Old It Is
blocks.text: There is a claim about lobsters that circulates online every few years: lobsters are biologically immortal. They do not age. They only die when something kills them. The claim is wrong, but it is wrong in an interesting way, and how it fails tells you more than how it spreads. Start with what is true. In most animals, including you, the machinery of the body wears down on a schedule. Cells divide a limited number of times. Protective caps on the ends of chromosomes, called telomeres, shorten with every division until the cell can no longer copy itself. Tissue thins. Repair slows. Fertility drops. Biologists call this senescence, and in humans it shows up as decades of gradually rising risk: the chance of dying at eighty is far higher than at thirty. Lobsters seem to skip much of that. They produce telomerase, an enzyme that rebuilds telomeres, and they produce it throughout their bodies rather than in a few tissues only. A lobster does not stop growing. A forty-year-old female is not less fertile than a fifteen-year-old female. She is more fertile, because she is larger, and she carries more eggs. Researchers describe this pattern as negligible senescence: not the absence of aging, but aging so slow it is hard to measure against the noise. Now the part the internet leaves out. Lobsters die, and they die of being lobsters. Growth requires molting, and molting is expensive. The larger the animal, the more shell it has to build and the more energy the escape demands. Old lobsters sometimes fail partway out and die inside the shell they were trying to leave. Others survive the molt and are eaten while soft. Many contract shell disease, a bacterial infection that eats into the exoskeleton faster than the animal can shed it. The lobster's biology does not schedule its death. Its body plan does. We are not even certain how long they live. You cannot count rings in a lobster the way you count rings in a tree, because it throws its skeleton away several times a decade. Age estimates lean on growth rates and on lipofuscin, a pigment that builds up in nerve tissue over time. Both are rough. The usual estimate is that some lobsters reach fifty or a hundred years, but the honest answer is that nobody has watched one from hatching to death. There is a smaller mystery worth noticing. A living lobster is mottled brown, olive, and blue, camouflage for a rocky sea floor. The red you picture is not the animal. It is chemistry. A protein called crustacyanin wraps around a red-orange pigment called astaxanthin and holds it in a bent shape that reflects dark blue-green. Heat unfolds the protein. The pigment springs back to its natural shape and shows its true color. The lobster on a plate is not changing color. It is being unwrapped. That is the pattern in all of this. The exciting story, the immortal lobster, is almost always a real fact stripped of its conditions. Telomerase is real. Negligible senescence is real. Neither one means the animal cannot die of old age, only that its clock runs differently, and that its ending is written by its shell rather than by its cells. The truth is stranger than the meme, and it is harder to fit on a screenshot.
